MHHS2401 · Week 4 · Anatomy of the Hand — Dr Mirjana Strkalj

Anatomy of the hand — bones, joints, muscles & fascia

The hand decoded the way it's built: the 27 bones and the carpal tunnel they form, the joints that classify by the movement they allow, the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles (and the nerves that run them), and the fascial wrappings that turn tendons into a working grip. Built from the lecture, using Gray's own figures.

§0Bones · LO1

Bones of the hand

Twenty-seven bones in three groups — and the tunnel they build.

The hand has three sets of bones: 8 carpals (the wrist), 5 metacarpals (the palm, numbered I–V from the thumb), and 14 phalanges (the fingers — proximal, middle and distal; the thumb has no middle). Plate 0.1 colour-codes the three, and each long bone has a base (proximal) and a head (distal).

Label Key — three groups of bones
Carpals
Eight small wrist bones in two rows — the foundation of the hand.
Metacarpals (I–V)
The five palm bones, numbered from the thumb (I) laterally; each has a base, shaft and head ("knuckle").
Proximal / middle / distal phalanges
The finger bones — three per finger, but only two in the thumb (no middle phalanx).

The carpal bones

Plate 0.2 names all eight. They sit in two rows. Proximal row (radial → ulnar): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform. Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. On radiographs the carpals aren't visible at birth — the capitate ossifies first (1–3 months), the rest following in an anticlockwise order.

Label Key — proximal & distal rows
Scaphoid · Lunate · Triquetrum · Pisiform
The proximal row (radial→ulnar). The scaphoid and lunate articulate with the radius at the wrist; the pisiform is a sesamoid sitting on the triquetrum.
Trapezium · Trapezoid · Capitate · Hamate
The distal row. The trapezium carries the thumb's saddle joint; the capitate is central and largest; the hamate's hook helps roof the tunnel.
Memory hook · the eight carpals

"Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle" — Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform · Trapezium, Trapezoid, Capitate, Hamate (proximal row first, radial→ulnar).

§0.1The carpal tunnel

The carpal bones don't lie flat — they form a bony arch, concave anteriorly, closed over by the flexor retinaculum to make the carpal tunnel just distal to the wrist. Plate 0.3 shows what runs through it: 9 tendons + 1 nerve — the 4 tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, the 4 of flexor digitorum profundus, the 1 tendon of flexor pollicis longus, and the median nerve.

Label Key — inside vs outside the tunnel
Carpal arch + flexor retinaculum
The bony floor/walls and fibrous roof that enclose the tunnel.
FDS + FDP tendons (8)
The long finger flexors passing to the digits.
Flexor pollicis longus tendon (1)
The thumb's long flexor — the 9th tendon.
Median nerve
The only nerve in the tunnel, lying just deep to the retinaculum — the structure squeezed in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Outside the tunnel
Extensor tendons, radial artery, and the ulnar nerve (in Guyon's canal, not the carpal tunnel) — all spared by carpal tunnel compression.
Reasoning · why an arch, not a plate

Curving the carpal row into an arch does two jobs at once. It deepens the palm so the hand can cup around objects, and it creates a protected conduit — the tunnel — that keeps the nine long flexor tendons and the median nerve on a controlled course into the hand rather than bowstringing across the wrist when you flex. The flexor retinaculum is the tie-beam that holds the arch's shape. Form (an arch) follows function (grip + a safe tendon path).

Clinical / real-world · carpal tunnel syndrome & the scaphoid

Because the tunnel is a rigid box, any swelling raises pressure and compresses its softest occupant — the median nerve. That's carpal tunnel syndrome: numbness/tingling over the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger, and thenar weakness — sparing the little finger (ulnar territory, outside the tunnel). Bones matter too: the scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal (a fall on the outstretched hand), and because its blood supply enters distally, a fracture can starve the proximal fragment — avascular necrosis.

R Recall checklist — bones
  • 27 bones — 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals (I–V), 14 phalanges (thumb has no middle).
  • Carpals — proximal: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ("Some Lovers Try Positions…").
  • Ossification — capitate first (1–3 months), then anticlockwise.
  • Carpal tunnel — bony arch + flexor retinaculum roof; contents = 9 tendons (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) + median nerve.
§1Joints · LO2

Joints of the hand

Classify each joint by its shape, and its movements follow.

From wrist to fingertip the joints step down in mobility, and each joint's type predicts its movements. Plate 1.1 maps the levels — from the distal radioulnar joint, through the wrist and midcarpal joints, to the carpometacarpal joints.

Label Key — from distal to proximal
Carpometacarpal joint
Between the distal carpal row and the metacarpal bases.
Intercarpal joints
Between adjacent carpals — small gliding joints.
Midcarpal joint
Between the proximal and distal carpal rows.
Wrist (radiocarpal) joint
Between the radius/articular disc and the proximal carpal row — the main wrist joint.
Distal radioulnar joint
Between radius and ulna — pronation/supination, not a hand joint proper.

Wrist, intercarpal & midcarpal

The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is a condyloid synovial joint between the distal radius + articular disc and the proximal carpal row (except the pisiform). Its fibrous capsule is thickened into the palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments and the ulnar/radial collateral ligaments, and it moves in flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction. The intercarpal joints are plane synovial (a little gliding), and the midcarpal joint between the two rows assists extension and abduction, complementing the radiocarpal joint.

§1.1Carpometacarpal & the thumb's saddle

The carpometacarpal (CMC) joints of the medial 4 digits are plane synovial with gliding movement that increases toward the little finger — which is why the 5th metacarpal slides visibly when you make a fist. The thumb is the exception: its CMC is a saddle synovial joint between the trapezium and the base of the 1st metacarpal (Plate 1.2), and that saddle shape is what gives the thumb its uniquely wide range — including opposition.

Label Key — the saddle
Trapezium & base of 1st metacarpal
The two saddle surfaces — each concave in one direction, convex in the other, fitting like a rider on a saddle.
Capsule with radial collateral ligament
The loose capsule and its ligaments — loose enough to permit the thumb's wide arc.
Anterior oblique ligament / palmar tubercle
A key stabiliser running to the palmar tubercle of the trapezium.
Saddle shape → opposition
Two perpendicular axes of movement let the thumb flex/extend, abduct/adduct and rotate to oppose the fingers.

§1.2Metacarpophalangeal & interphalangeal joints

The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints of the medial 4 digits are condyloid synovial joints allowing flexion, extension, abduction and adduction. They're held by collateral ligaments (which fuse anteriorly into the palmar ligament) and, for digits 2–5, by deep transverse metacarpal ligaments that tie the metacarpal heads together (Plate 1.3). The interphalangeal (IP) joints — proximal and distal — are hinge synovial joints, so they only flex and extend.

Label Key — holding the fingers together
Deep transverse metacarpal ligaments
Tie the heads of metacarpals 2–5 together, so the fingers move as a unit (and can't splay apart).
Collateral ligaments
Side ligaments of the MCP/IP joints; they tighten in flexion, limiting side-to-side movement of a bent finger.
Palmar ligament
The anterior fusion of the collateral ligaments — the volar plate.
Capsule of the MCP joint
Encloses the condyloid joint that permits flexion/extension + abduction/adduction.
Reasoning · shape dictates movement

Run down the hand and every joint's freedom is written in its shape. The condyloid wrist and MCP joints are egg-in-socket — two axes, so flex/extend and abduct/adduct, but no true rotation. The saddle thumb CMC adds enough rotational play for opposition — the single feature that makes the human hand a precision tool. The hinge IP joints are pure one-axis flexion/extension, trading mobility for the stability a fingertip needs to press. Name the joint type and you've named its movements.

Clinical / real-world · rheumatoid arthritis

These synovial joints are the target of rheumatoid arthritis — a chronic autoimmune disease (~1 in 50 Australians, more common in women) that inflames synovium and preferentially attacks the small joints of the hand and feet. As the MCP joints and their ligaments erode, the fingers drift into the classic ulnar deviation and can dislocate (Plate 1.4). It's a direct clinical read-out of the ligamentous anatomy above — when the collateral and transverse ligaments fail, the fingers lose their alignment.

Label Key — the radiographic signs
MCP ulnar deviation
The fingers drift toward the ulnar side as MCP ligaments fail.
Erosive change / sclerotic borders
Chronic joint-margin erosion, most prominent around the MCP joints.
Dislocation
Advanced disease subluxes/dislocates the joints entirely.
R Recall checklist — joints
  • Wrist (radiocarpal) — condyloid; radius + disc / proximal row (not pisiform); flex/ext/abd/add/circumduction.
  • Intercarpal plane (gliding); midcarpal aids extension & abduction.
  • CMC — medial 4 plane; thumb = saddle (trapezium + 1st MC base) → opposition.
  • MCP — condyloid + collateral/palmar/deep transverse metacarpal ligaments; IP — hinge (flex/ext).
  • Rheumatoid arthritis — autoimmune synovial disease; small hand joints; MCP ulnar deviation.
§2Muscles · LO3

Muscles of the hand

Extrinsic power from the forearm, intrinsic precision in the palm.

The hand is moved by two muscle sets: extrinsic muscles whose bellies sit in the forearm and pull on the hand by long tendons (power), and intrinsic muscles wholly within the hand (fine control). Start with the extrinsics.

Extrinsic muscles of the hand (forearm bellies, long tendons)
LayerAnterior (flexor/pronator)Posterior (extensor)
SuperficialPronator teres · flexor carpi radialis (FCR) · palmaris longus (PL) · flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU)Extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) · extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) · extensor digitorum (ED) · extensor digiti minimi (EDM) · extensor carpi ulnaris (ECU)
IntermediateFlexor digitorum superficialis (FDS)—
DeepFlexor digitorum profundus (FDP) · flexor pollicis longus (FPL) · pronator quadratusSupinator · abductor pollicis longus (APL) · extensor pollicis brevis (EPB) · extensor pollicis longus (EPL) · extensor indicis (EI)

§2.1Intrinsic muscles & their innervation

The intrinsic muscles fall into groups by region and action:

Intrinsic muscles of the hand
GroupMusclesNerve
Thenar (thumb)Abductor pollicis brevis · flexor pollicis brevis · opponens pollicisMedian
Hypothenar (little finger)Abductor digiti minimi · flexor digiti minimi · opponens digiti minimiUlnar
Adductor pollicis(transverse + oblique heads)Ulnar
Lumbricals (4)From FDP tendons → extensor hoods: flex MCP, extend IPLateral 2 median · medial 2 ulnar
Dorsal interossei (4)ABduct the fingers (DAB)Ulnar
Palmar interossei (3)ADduct the fingers (PAD)Ulnar
Palmaris brevisPalmar aponeurosis → skin; improves gripUlnar

The unifying rule: the ulnar nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except the thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals, which are median.

Plate 2.1 and Plate 2.2 contrast the two sets of interossei — the ones that spread the fingers and the ones that draw them back together.

Label Key — the abductors
Dorsal interossei (4)
Arise from adjacent metacarpal shafts (bipennate); insert into the extensor hood + base of proximal phalanx.
Action — ABduction
DAB: they spread the index, middle and ring fingers away from the midline (the middle finger).
First dorsal interosseous
The large muscle in the thumb web; the radial artery dives between its heads to enter the palm.
Label Key — the adductors
Palmar interossei (3)
Arise from a single metacarpal shaft (unipennate); insert into the extensor hoods.
Action — ADduction
PAD: they pull the fingers toward the midline (draw them together).
Together with lumbricals
Via the extensor hoods, the interossei also help flex MCP and extend IP joints — the "intrinsic-plus" position.
Memory hook · nerves & interossei

DAB = Dorsal ABduct · PAD = Palmar ADduct. Median hand muscles = "MEat LOAF": Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis. Everything else intrinsic = ulnar.

Reasoning · why the median exceptions matter

The ulnar-nerve-except-("MEat LOAF") split isn't trivia — it's why hand-nerve lesions look so different. Lose the ulnar nerve and you lose most intrinsics: the interossei and medial lumbricals fail, so the MCP joints hyperextend and the IP joints claw — the ulnar claw, worst in the little and ring fingers (whose lumbricals are ulnar). Lose the median nerve (e.g. at the carpal tunnel) and the thenar muscles waste, flattening the thumb into the plane of the palm — the ape hand, unable to oppose. The nerve supply predicts the deformity.

Clinical / real-world · lumbricals & the "intrinsic-plus" hand

The lumbricals are anatomically odd — they arise from a tendon (flexor digitorum profundus) and insert into another (the extensor hood). That lets them do something no other muscle can: flex the MCP joint while extending the IP joints, the position that lets you write or hold a card flat. When intrinsics are paralysed the hand loses exactly this, defaulting to the clawed "intrinsic-minus" posture — which is why the lumbricals and interossei are tested directly in any hand-nerve exam.

R Recall checklist — muscles
  • Extrinsic — forearm bellies, long tendons; anterior (flexors/pronators) + posterior (extensors) in superficial/intermediate/deep layers.
  • Intrinsic — thenar, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, 4 lumbricals, 4 dorsal + 3 palmar interossei, palmaris brevis.
  • Innervation — ULNAR except thenar + lateral 2 lumbricals (median: "MEat LOAF").
  • Interossei — DAB (dorsal abduct), PAD (palmar adduct).
  • Lumbricals — FDP tendon → extensor hood; flex MCP + extend IP.
§3Fascia · LO4

Fascia of the hand

The wrappings that turn loose tendons into a working grip.

Muscles and bones need connective-tissue scaffolding to work. The hand's fascia has five parts: the palmar aponeurosis, flexor retinaculum, fibrous digital sheaths, extensor retinaculum and extensor hoods — each keeping tendons on task.

Palmar aponeurosis & flexor retinaculum

The palmar aponeurosis (Plate 3.1) is a strong, well-defined thickening of the palm's deep fascia. Its apex blends with the palmaris longus tendon; distally it splits into four longitudinal bands that become continuous with the fibrous digital sheaths. It facilitates grip and protects the neurovascular structures beneath. The flexor retinaculum (from §0) forms the roof of the carpal tunnel and limits anterior movement of the long flexor tendons.

Label Key — the palmar fascia
Longitudinal fibres
Four bands running to the digits, continuous with the fibrous digital sheaths — anchor the skin for grip.
Transverse fibres
Cross-struts binding the longitudinal bands together.
Palmaris brevis muscle
A small skin muscle over the hypothenar eminence that tightens the aponeurosis to improve grip.

Extensor retinaculum & extensor hoods

On the back of the wrist, the extensor retinaculum holds the long extensor tendons down and sends septa to bone forming 6 separate tunnels, each with synovial-sheathed tendons (Plate 3.2). Over the fingers, the extensor tendons flatten into extensor hoods — expansions of extensor digitorum and extensor pollicis longus (Plate 3.3) — onto which the lumbricals and interossei insert.

Label Key — six compartments
Extensor retinaculum
The dorsal wrist band that stops the extensor tendons bowstringing when you extend the wrist.
6 tunnels (section B)
Septa to the radius/ulna divide the space into 6 osteofibrous compartments (e.g. 1 = APL/EPB, 2 = ECRL/ECRB, 3 = EPL, 4 = ED/EI, 5 = EDM, 6 = ECU).
Synovial sheaths
Line each tunnel to let the tendons glide with minimal friction.
Label Key — how the hood works
Extensor hood
The flattened aponeurotic expansion of ED (and EPL) that wraps the dorsum of the finger.
Fulcrums at MCP & IP joints
The hood crosses each joint, so a single pull is distributed across all three.
Intrinsic pull
Lumbricals/interossei insert into the hood — contracting them flexes the MCP and extends the IP joints.

§3.1Fibrous digital sheaths

Along the fingers, fibrous digital sheaths are ligamentous tubes enclosing the synovial sheaths and the tendons of the superficial and deep flexors (and flexor pollicis longus). They limit anterior and side-to-side movement and reduce friction; the synovial lining lets the tendons glide smoothly.

Reasoning · one job, five wrappings — no bowstringing

Every piece of hand fascia solves the same mechanical problem: a tendon takes the shortest path, which across a bending joint means lifting off the bone (bowstringing) and losing power. The retinacula (flexor and extensor) and the fibrous digital sheaths are tie-downs that hold the tendons against the skeleton so their pull stays efficient, while synovial sheaths cut the friction that tethering would otherwise create. Grip is as much about these restraints as about the muscles themselves.

Clinical / real-world · tenosynovitis & mallet finger

Tenosynovitis — inflammation of a tendon and its synovial sheath — swells the digit and makes movement painful; because the digital sheaths connect to the common flexor sheath, an infection can track from a fingertip up into the palm and wrist. And the extensor hood has its own signature injury: forcibly flexing an extended fingertip avulses the terminal extensor slip, leaving a drooping DIP joint that can't straighten — mallet (baseball) finger.

R Recall checklist — fascia
  • Five parts — palmar aponeurosis, flexor retinaculum, fibrous digital sheaths, extensor retinaculum, extensor hoods.
  • Palmar aponeurosis — blends with palmaris longus; 4 bands → digital sheaths; grip + protection.
  • Flexor retinaculum = carpal-tunnel roof; limits flexor-tendon bowstringing.
  • Extensor retinaculum — 6 synovial-sheathed tunnels.
  • Extensor hoods — expansions of ED + EPL; injury = mallet finger.
  • Fibrous digital sheaths — enclose flexor tendons + synovial sheath; tenosynovitis = painful swelling.
